summary:
Nauru decriminalised consensual same-sex conduct in 2016. The provisions repealed were sections of a criminal code inherited from Queensland in 1899, and the repeal also covered the attempted-suicide offences that sat alongside them. A visitor should not expect prosecution for consensual same-sex intimacy under Nauruan law.

The legal position for trans and intersex visitors is markedly thinner. Kaleidoscope Trust's country assessment records that intersex and transgender people in Nauru have no explicit legal recognition or protection, that same-sex marriages and unions remain illegal, and that there is no employment-discrimination protection for lesbian, bisexual, trans and intersex people.

No source in this inventory documents how Nauru handles gender markers on passports or other identity documents. A visitor cannot assume that a Nauruan-issued document will reflect a stated identity, and no consular or immigration screening procedure for trans travellers is described anywhere in these sources.

The one gender-identity provision located for Nauru operates inside immigration detention. The Nauru Regional Processing Centre Rules 2014, made under the Asylum Seekers (Regional Processing Centre) Act 2012, prohibit discrimination against any person on the basis of sex or gender, sexual preference or gender identity within the regional processing facility. That protection is confined to the immigration-detention estate. It does not reach Nauru's criminal-justice prison system, and it addresses non-discrimination rather than questions of housing by birth sex versus identity, special units or solitary confinement.

Nauru's diplomatic position has at points favoured protection. In 2011 it was among 84 countries signing a joint statement on ending acts of violence based on sexual orientation and gender identity, delivered by Colombia, alongside Fiji, the Marshall Islands, Micronesia and others.
tangentialFactors:
The independent Vexen LGBT Equality Index (Human Truth Foundation, 2025) places Nauru 101st with a score of -0.10, far below the top-ranked countries at 4.88 and below most of its Pacific neighbours. The index is a comparative ranking rather than a legal instrument, and its methodology is not set out in these sources.

Nauru's last CEDAW state report, submitted in 2016, contained no LBTI-specific information, so there is no multilateral review record in this inventory against which to test the country's treatment of trans people. The 2016 decriminalisation is documented by contemporaneous reporting but no source here records subsequent litigation, enforcement practice or a stated government policy on gender recognition.
localsOnly:
Residents have no statutory employment-discrimination protection on grounds of sexual orientation, gender identity or intersex status, according to Kaleidoscope Trust's assessment, and same-sex marriages and unions remain prohibited.

Transgender and intersex Nauruans have no explicit legal recognition: there is no sourced mechanism for changing or aligning a legal gender marker, and no anti-discrimination statute naming gender identity outside the immigration-detention rules.

The non-discrimination duty attached to the Nauru Regional Processing Centre Rules 2014 binds conduct inside that facility only. People held in Nauru's corrections system fall outside it, and no data was found on where transgender prisoners are housed or on any trans-prisoner case or ruling.

The 2011 joint statement on sexual orientation and gender identity remains the clearest documented instance of Nauru taking a protective position in a multilateral forum.
outOfScopeNotes:
Unresolved: no source in the inventory addresses gender markers on Nauruan passports or identity documents, nor any entry, visa or airport-screening practice that could disclose a trans traveller's status. The absence is a gap in these sources, not evidence that no rule exists.

Unresolved: whether the regional processing centre's gender-identity non-discrimination clause has ever been invoked, and how it is enforced in practice, is not sourced here. The same is true of any complaint mechanism available to a trans detainee.

Unresolved: no documentation was found on housing placement for transgender prisoners in Nauru's corrections system, and no trans-prisoner case or judicial ruling is recorded in these materials.

Unresolved: the inventory does not show whether Nauru maintains any statutory pathway for legal gender recognition, or whether the 2016 CEDAW report omission on LBTI matters was raised by the treaty committee.
